approachQuestion.prompt:
Refill Recipes

Given distinct positive integer portion sizes sizes and target T, return every multiset of portions summing to T. Any size may be used any number of times. Represent a recipe by a nondecreasing list of sizes, and return each once, in any order.

Examples:
sizes=[5,2,3], T=7 -> [[2,2,3],[2,5]].
sizes=[4,6], T=5 -> [].

Constraints: 1 <= d=sizes.length <= 8; 1 <= sizes[i] <= 20; 1 <= T <= 40. The input may be unsorted and must not be modified.

options.text: Sort a copy and explore fitting sizes in nondecreasing index order. After choosing index i, recurse with i still eligible, then remove the chosen portion on return.
options.feedback: Keeping i eligible implements unlimited reuse. Nondecreasing indices remove order duplicates; positive sizes guarantee progress toward the target.

options.text: After choosing size i, recurse with only indices strictly greater than i.
options.feedback: For sizes=[2,3], T=7, this misses [2,2,3] because it forbids the second 2.

options.text: Allow all sizes again after every choice and emit every completed list.
options.feedback: For sizes=[2,3], T=5, [2,3] and [3,2] are the same multiset and must not both be returned.

options.text: Enumerate every ordered sequence of portions that does not exceed T, sort each successful sequence, and deduplicate the recipes in an ordered set.
options.feedback: This is correct but explores all orderings of the same recipe. Nondecreasing eligibility prevents that redundant search.

feedback.reason: Keeping i eligible implements unlimited reuse. Nondecreasing indices remove order duplicates; positive sizes guarantee progress toward the target.
details: Make a sorted copy of sizes. Carry the first eligible index and remaining target. For each eligible size that fits, append it and recurse with that same index, then undo. Stop the candidate loop at the first size above the remainder. Copy the path at remainder zero.

Sorted sizes permit ending the candidate loop when a size exceeds the remainder. Recurse from the same index to allow reuse, but never earlier indices, which would duplicate permutations of one recipe.

“Sort a copy and explore fitting sizes in nondecreasing index order. After choosing index i, recurse with i still eligible, then remove the chosen portion on return.”: Keeping i eligible implements unlimited reuse. Nondecreasing indices remove order duplicates; positive sizes guarantee progress toward the target.
“After choosing size i, recurse with only indices strictly greater than i.”: For sizes=[2,3], T=7, this misses [2,2,3] because it forbids the second 2.
“Allow all sizes again after every choice and emit every completed list.”: For sizes=[2,3], T=5, [2,3] and [3,2] are the same multiset and must not both be returned.

“Enumerate every ordered sequence of portions that does not exceed T, sort each successful sequence, and deduplicate the recipes in an ordered set.”: This is correct but explores all orderings of the same recipe. Nondecreasing eligibility prevents that redundant search.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze `acm-b18-16-search` only. Let C count all candidate-loop iterations over the whole search, and R count portion entries copied into results. Sort a d-entry copy with an in-place comparison sort using a linear-size scratch allowance; let b=min(sizes). The longest branch has at most floor(T/b) portions. Include root and sorting work. Choose the tightest stated time and auxiliary-space pair. Count recursion and mutable working state; exclude supplied input and returned output storage, but include copying work in time. Primitive integer/index operations and preallocated-array updates cost constant time; dynamic appends are amortized constant time. No hashing is used unless explicitly stated.

options.text: O(d log(d+1) + C + R) time, O(d + T/b) auxiliary space
O(d log(d+1) + C + R) time, O(d) auxiliary space
O(d log(d+1) + d·C + R) time, O(d + T/b) auxiliary space
O(T+d+R) time, O(d + T/b) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Sort once, then count candidate trials and copied completed recipes.
details: Sorting costs d log(d+1) in the comparison-sort worst case. Every nonroot call follows a candidate trial, so C accounts for recursive overhead; output copies add R. The root constant is absorbed by d>=1.
The copied/sort workspace uses d entries; path and recursion use at most T/b entries/frames, attained by repeatedly choosing a smallest size before finishing or failing.

Let C count all candidate-loop iterations over the whole search, and R count portion entries copied into results. Sort a d-entry copy with an in-place comparison sort using a linear-size scratch allowance; let b=min(sizes). The longest branch has at most floor(T/b) portions. Include root and sorting work.
“O(d log(d+1) + C + R) time, O(d) auxiliary space”: Unlimited reuse can make the path much longer than d.
“O(d log(d+1) + d·C + R) time, O(d + T/b) auxiliary space”: C already counts candidate iterations, so multiplying by d double-counts them.
“O(T+d+R) time, O(d + T/b) auxiliary space”: Many different partial recipes can be searched; this is not a single pass over target values.
